title: Work and public-benefit reliance can coexist within the same labor system
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office GAO-26-108703; Census estimates for 2024 labor characteristics and selected state administrative employer analysis through September 2025
geography: United States national estimates plus selected data from 15 state agencies across 11 states

observations.period: 2024; adults ages 19–64 enrolled in Medicaid who worked at some point

denominator.unit: adults ages 19–64 enrolled in Medicaid; GAO national Census estimate

full_time_share.unit: approximate percent of working adults working 35 or more hours per week

annual_attachment.value: less likely than nonprogram wage earners to work full-time hours for 50 or more weeks

observations.method: GAO analysis of Census data on working-age Medicaid enrollees and labor characteristics.
observations.uncertainty: Worked at some point is not stable employment, adequate earnings, predictable scheduling, continuous coverage, or benefit receipt by the worker personally; the comparison does not identify selection or causality.
observations.subgroup: Adults ages 19–64 enrolled in Medicaid who worked at some point in 2024.
observations.counterinterpretation: Medicaid coverage may protect against medical-cost exposure and support work, while low wages, household composition, health, or job conditions may jointly shape eligibility; employment alone does not show independence or dependence.

observations.period: 2024; adults ages 19–64 living in SNAP-receiving households who worked at some point

denominator.unit: adults ages 19–64 living in SNAP-receiving households; GAO national Census estimate

full_time_share.unit: approximate percent of working adults working 35 or more hours per week

annual_attachment.value: less likely than nonprogram wage earners to work full-time hours for 50 or more weeks

observations.method: GAO analysis of Census data on adults in SNAP-receiving households and labor characteristics.
observations.uncertainty: SNAP is measured at the household level; the worker need not be the benefit recipient or decision-maker. The estimates do not show benefit amount, adequacy, eligibility churn, schedule control, or causality.
observations.subgroup: Adults ages 19–64 living in SNAP-receiving households who worked at some point in 2024.
observations.counterinterpretation: Household SNAP receipt can coexist with work because wages, food needs, family composition, health costs, and hours do not align into a single independence measure; program use does not establish employer responsibility.

observations.period: September 2025 selected-state administrative employer analysis; report reissued August 24, 2026

denominator.unit: state agencies across 11 states supplying selected employer data; nondisabled, nonelderly working adults for the employer component

cross_state_top_employer_companies.unit: companies among top 25 employers of Medicaid enrollees or SNAP beneficiaries in at least two states

fortune_500_subset.unit: companies among the 50 largest Fortune 500 employers by employee count

program_and_occupation_context.value: workers concentrated in transportation, restaurants/food preparation, and retail sales; employer identities and state rankings vary

observations.method: GAO analysis of employer data obtained from 15 state agencies across 11 states as of September 2025; employer results are separate from national Census estimates.
observations.uncertainty: Top-employer overlap is a concentration signal, not a national ranking, per-worker incidence, compensation comparison, employer policy finding, or evidence of benefit shifting; definitions and coverage vary by state and the report was revised for Rhode Island figures.
observations.subgroup: Nondisabled, nonelderly working adult Medicaid enrollees and working adults in SNAP-receiving households in the selected administrative data.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large employers can appear because of workforce size, occupation, place, or sector composition rather than intentional low compensation or public-benefit reliance; worker choice, wages, hours, employer coverage, turnover, and benefit continuity are not joined.

related_sources.claim: Official GAO report page supplies national estimates, selected-state employer scope, findings, methods, and August 24, 2026 revision note.

boundary: This record establishes a mixed-universe labor and public-benefit interaction: work, safety-net participation, private-sector concentration, occupational composition, and selected-state employer overlap. It does not establish wages, schedule control, employer intent, benefit shifting, eligibility churn, household security, worker alternatives, remedy, trust, political action, or exit.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GAO HTML report page retrieved and hashed; report PDF and state administrative files not retained
